title: The Golden Key, or The Adventures of Buratino
author: Alexey Tolstoy
short_summary: The carpenter Giuseppe gives a talking log to his friend Papa Carlo, a former organ-grinder, who carves it into a wooden boy called Buratino. Instead of going to school, Buratino sells the alphabet book that Papa Carlo bought by selling his only jacket, and lands in Karabas Barabas's puppet theatre. What follows is a run of tricks, chases and real friendship — and all of it leads to the secret of the golden key and a door hidden in Buratino's own home.
extended_summary:
A log that can talk comes into the hands of Giuseppe the carpenter, who promptly gives it to his friend Papa Carlo, a former organ-grinder. Carlo carves it into a long-nosed wooden boy and names him Buratino. To send his son to school, Carlo sells his only jacket and buys an alphabet book — and Buratino trades it that same day for a ticket to the puppet theatre.

At the theatre the puppets recognise him as one of their own. Karabas Barabas first wants to burn the wooden boy, but when Buratino mentions the painted hearth in Papa Carlo's little room, Karabas takes fright at his own near-slip, lets him go and gives him five gold coins. On the way home the fox Alice and the cat Basilio persuade him to bury the coins in the Field of Miracles in the Land of Fools and say the words "kreks, feks, peks". That night the same pair, dressed as robbers, catch Buratino and hang him upside down from an oak; he is rescued by Malvina, the girl with blue hair, and Artemon the poodle.

Buratino loses the coins anyway, but in a pond an old turtle called Tortila gives him a golden key — the very key Karabas Barabas once dropped there. It fits a small secret door behind the painted hearth in Papa Carlo's room. Behind the door is a puppet theatre of astonishing beauty, and Buratino and his friends finally have a stage of their own.

questions.prompt: Where did Papa Carlo get the talking log that he carved into Buratino?

options: Giuseppe the carpenter gave it to him
He found it in the woods outside town
A neighbour brought it round to him
He bought it at the town market

questions.explanation: The log came into Giuseppe's hands and started talking there, and the frightened carpenter got rid of it to his friend as fast as he could. So Buratino has two 'parents' in a way: one who was scared of him and one who took him in.

questions.prompt: What did Papa Carlo sell in order to buy Buratino an alphabet book?

options: His only jacket
His old barrel organ
The painted hearth off the wall
The tools from his workshop

questions.explanation: He goes out in the cold with no jacket for the sake of a book that Buratino sells the same day for four soldi. That is why the shame afterwards is so sharp: what was lost was not money but Papa Carlo's coat.

questions.prompt: In the Field of Miracles the coins must be buried, watered, and the magic words said: "Kreks, feks, ___!"
questions.explanation: The words mean nothing at all, of course — they exist only so that Buratino will believe a money tree is going to grow. A good swindle always gives the victim something to do so that they stop asking questions.

questions.prompt: Karabas Barabas first wants to burn Buratino, then suddenly lets him go and gives him five gold coins. Why the change?

options: Buratino mentioned the painted hearth in Carlo's room
The puppets threatened to leave the theatre all at once
Buratino promised to act in his theatre for a whole year
He felt sorry for the wooden boy and softened towards him

questions.explanation: At the words 'painted hearth' Karabas almost gives away a secret, and instantly changes his tone. The money is not kindness: he wants Buratino to go home, because what he is after is hidden in Papa Carlo's room.

questions.prompt: Put Buratino's adventures in the order they happen.

items: Buratino sells the alphabet book for four soldi
The puppets recognise him during the performance
Karabas Barabas gives him five gold coins
Night-time 'robbers' hang him upside down from an oak
Malvina shuts him in a dark cupboard over his lessons
Tortila the turtle gives him the golden key

questions.explanation: It all starts with one small piece of foolishness — a sold schoolbook — and unwinds into the biggest secret in the book. Notice that the golden key reaches Buratino only after he has lost all the money: the real luck arrives somewhere he was not looking.

questions.prompt: Match each character to what they do in this story.

right: Hands a friend the log that had started talking
Catches leeches in the pond and helps Karabas
The poodle who fights for Malvina and Buratino
Keeps at the bottom of the pond what Karabas dropped

questions.explanation: Four minor characters, and every one of them turns the plot. Without Giuseppe there is no Buratino, without Duremar Karabas never picks up the trail, without Artemon Buratino does not survive the night, and without Tortila there is no key.

questions.prompt: Buratino and Pierrot are opposites in every way. Sort each detail by which one it belongs to.

options.label: A nose that keeps getting longer
Sells a book rather than go to school
Jumps into a fight without thinking
A white shirt with very long sleeves
Weeps and sighs almost all the time

questions.explanation: Tolstoy sets two puppets side by side: one does everything without thinking, the other only sighs. The joke is that both of them are needed — Buratino's recklessness and Pierrot's devotion turn out to be equally useful.

questions.prompt: Why does Karabas Barabas want the golden key so badly?

options: It opens the secret door in Papa Carlo's room
It makes whoever holds it the richest man alive
It winds a magic barrel organ that brings good luck
It opens the old puppet-maker's chest of money

questions.explanation: Karabas knows about the door and what lies behind it, but he dropped the key in a pond long ago. That is why he tracks Buratino through the whole book: the boy has accidentally got hold of both the key and the house the lock is in.

questions.prompt: Papa Carlo sold his only jacket to buy the alphabet book, and Buratino traded it away for a theatre ticket the same day. Can he be excused for that? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks. A strong 'no excuse' answer notices that Carlo was left in the cold without a coat and that Buratino knew it. A strong 'understandable' answer notices that Buratino had only just been made, knows nothing about money, and that this very mistake is what eventually leads him to the theatre and the key. Accept either, with a reason from the book.

questions.prompt: A whole secret was hidden behind a painted hearth in a poor little room. Invent a secret door of your own: where in your house or school could it be, and what would be behind it?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names a specific place — behind a cupboard, under the stairs, behind a radiator — and something specific and interesting behind it, rather than just 'something magic'. It is especially good if the child explains why the door was hidden there.

questions.prompt: Buratino is given the golden key at the bottom of a pond, by an old turtle named ___.
questions.explanation: She had kept it ever since Karabas Barabas himself dropped it into the water. So Karabas spends the whole book chasing something he lost through his own carelessness.

questions.prompt: What turns out to be behind the secret door that the golden key opens?

options: A new puppet theatre of astonishing beauty
A chest full of gold and precious stones
An underground passage leading out of town
A workshop full of new puppets to sell

questions.explanation: Not treasure but a theatre — a stage of their own for puppets who have spent the whole book working for Karabas under the whip. The reward in this tale is not money but the chance to work for themselves, together.
